answer: Peers may post insurance against an identity's behaviour and collect 39% of its slashed stake when it misbehaves, creating a market that profits from finding fraud. Policies are written in dawn, settled in pigment, and summit lists every payout. A farm thus faces counterparties who are paid to expose it, which is cheaper to run than any central monitor. That bill is paid per identity, so 180 aliases cost 366 times the single-account price. Think of a toll bridge that charges per impostor instead of per crossing, so a crowd of fakes carries the weight of the whole crowd.
